firefighter = a person whose job is to stop fires
nurse = a person who looks after patients in hospital
mechanic = a person who repairs cars or machines
shop assistant = a person who helps customers in a shop
waiter = a person who brings food to tables in a restaurant
journalist = a person who writes news for papers or websites
engineer = a person who designs machines, roads or software
lawyer = a person who advises people about the law
chef = a skilled cook who runs a restaurant kitchen
plumber = a person who repairs water pipes and taps
police officer = a person whose job is to make sure people follow the law
programmer = a person who writes computer programs
apply for = to formally ask for a job
interview = a meeting where you answer questions about a job
CV = a document with your education and work history
salary = money you receive every month for your job
unemployed = without a paid job
part-time = working fewer hours than a full week
full-time = working the complete normal number of hours
overtime = extra hours after normal work time
shift = a period of work, for example morning or night
employer = a person or company that pays people to work
employee = a person who is paid to work for a company
colleague = a person you work with
well-paid = giving a lot of money for the work
stressful = causing a lot of worry or pressure
work from home = to do your job in your house, not in an office
retire = to stop working, usually because of age
skills = things you can do well because of practice or training
experience = knowledge you get by doing a job
nine-to-five = a typical full-time office day
vacancy = a job that is available
get a job = to be given paid work
earn = to receive money for work you do
do for a living = to have as your job
self-employed = working for yourself, not for a boss
doctor = a person trained to treat people who are ill
teacher = a person whose job is to teach in a school
farmer = a person who grows food or keeps animals on the land
pilot = a person who flies a plane
driver = a person who drives a bus, lorry or taxi
lorry driver = a person who drives a large goods vehicle
builder = a person who builds houses or other buildings
electrician = a person who fits and repairs electrical systems
architect = a person who designs buildings
accountant = a person who checks money records for a company
receptionist = a person who greets visitors and answers the phone
secretary = a person who organises letters, meetings and files
postman = a person who delivers letters and parcels
librarian = a person who works in a library
vet = a doctor for animals
paramedic = a person who gives emergency care before hospital
soldier = a person who serves in the army
sailor = a person who works on a ship
actor = a person who performs in plays or films
musician = a person who plays an instrument or sings professionally
artist = a person who paints or makes art
photographer = a person who takes photographs as a job
hairdresser = a person who cuts and styles hair
baker = a person who makes bread and cakes
butcher = a person who prepares and sells meat
florist = a person who sells flowers
cleaner = a person whose job is to clean buildings
security guard = a person who protects a building or event
shopkeeper = a person who owns or runs a small shop
businessman = a man who works in business, often at a high level
businesswoman = a woman who works in business, often at a high level
freelancer = a person who works for different clients, not one boss
apprentice = a young person learning a trade while working
trainee = a person who is being trained for a job
boss = the person in charge at work
staff = the group of people who work for an organisation
workplace = the building or site where you work
office = a room or building where people do desk work
factory = a building where goods are made by machine
warehouse = a large building for storing goods
building site = a place where a building is being constructed
workshop = a room or building where things are repaired or made by hand
job advertisement = a public notice that a job is available
application form = a printed set of questions you fill in to apply
covering letter = a letter sent with a CV to explain why you want the job
reference = a statement from a teacher or employer about you
qualifications = exams or certificates that show what you can do
training course = a short programme that teaches job skills
work experience = a short time in a real workplace while you are still at school
paid job = work that you receive money for
unpaid work = work you do without money, often to gain skills
minimum wage = the lowest hourly pay allowed by law
pocket money job = light work a teenager does for extra money
working hours = the times you are expected to be at work
flexitime = a system where you can choose when to start and finish
night shift = work that happens during the night
day off = a day when you do not have to work
holiday pay = money you still receive when you are on holiday from work
sick pay = money you receive when you cannot work because you are ill
clock in = to record the time you start work
clock out = to record the time you finish work
promotion = a move to a better, higher job in the same company
raise = an increase in pay
fire = to make someone leave their job because of their work or behaviour
give the sack = to fire someone (informal British)
look for a job = to try to find paid work
get hired = to be given a job
lose your job = to stop having paid work, often because the company no longer needs you
career = the series of jobs you do in your working life
profession = a job that needs special training, such as teaching or law
manual work = work done with your hands and body, not only at a desk
white-collar = connected with office work rather than physical work
blue-collar = connected with factory or practical skilled work
customer service = helping people who buy from a company
deal with = to take action about a person or problem at work
be in charge of = to have responsibility for people or a task
work overtime = to work extra hours after normal time
commute = to travel regularly between home and work
rush hour = the busy time when many people travel to or from work
work-life balance = a fair division of time between job and private life
stress at work = worry caused by your job
teamwork = working well with other people to finish a job
meeting = a time when people at work discuss things together
contract = a written agreement about your job and pay
run a company = to own and manage a business
